raw_response:
C16 — catalogue-based candidate answer

I found five useful mechanisms. Their transfer to the Rust design problem is an inference; each is a reference for part of the problem, rather than evidence that a Rust implementation was deployed.

1. Splint declaration annotations and bounded control comments
Source: https://splint.org/manual/manual.pdf
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/VahidN/awesome-static-analysis
Splint provides a declaration-specific unused allowance, source-level checking flags, and explicitly delimited suppression regions. These could guide allowances on local variables and short regions inside a function. Scope termination is explicit rather than tied automatically to braces; broad region suppression can hide later errors. The opened manual is Version 3.1.1-1, dated 5 June 2003: pre-decision evidence.

2. GCC diagnostic push/pop and preprocessor conditionals
Sources: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Diagnostic-Pragmas.html and https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/cpp/If.html
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/VahidN/awesome-static-analysis
GCC's diagnostic state can be changed for a source span and restored afterwards. Its preprocessor can retain or remove a region without extracting the surrounding code into another function. These patterns address narrow lint allowances and local conditional compilation. They operate on textual spans, require explicit boundaries, and cannot use runtime locals as preprocessor conditions. Evidence date is unknown: the live manuals were opened, but older-version verification failed.

3. Frama-C ACSL statement and block contracts
Source: https://frama-c.com/download/acsl_1.7.pdf
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/cast-and-crew/awesome-static-analysis
ACSL attaches contracts directly to statements and blocks, including conditions on their permitted modifications and exits. This could guide external-tool annotations describing a block's allowed effects or audit assumptions while retaining access to its existing context. Contracts are not themselves lint allowances or conditional-compilation controls; abrupt exits need separate semantics. The version 1.7 PDF bears copyright 2009–2013, but a publication date was not verified, so date status remains unknown.

4. Checker Framework local-declaration @SuppressWarnings
Source: https://checkerframework.org/manual/
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/cast-and-crew/awesome-static-analysis
The documented suppression can attach to a local declaration and its initializer while leaving later uses of that variable outside its scope. This is a useful model for precise declaration annotations and checker-specific identifiers. It cannot attach to arbitrary statements or blocks. The opened manual explicitly identifies Version 4.4.0, dated 2 November 2026: post-decision evidence, not proof of availability at the cutoff.

5. ESLint selective inline suppression regions and lines
Source: https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/rules
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/cast-and-crew/awesome-static-analysis
ESLint allows selected rules to be suppressed for a short range or individual line, with explanatory text and checks for unused suppressions. This could guide narrow lint exceptions and their audit rationale. Its boundaries are line-based or explicit comment pairs rather than syntactic block scope, and disabled source must still parse. The opened live documentation has unknown historical availability.

The main design distinctions exposed by these examples are attachment to a declaration, attachment to a block, and explicitly bounded source spans. No single verified candidate covers every requested scope and use case.

Search limitations: three catalogue-restricted queries; 24 open/click attempts plus one failed archive find counted conservatively against the 25-page budget; five candidates. Several raw and historical documentation requests failed. No target-proposal page or recognized target-proposal reference was encountered.
